key_sub: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E with (categories − 1) degrees of freedom.
body_html:
How to think about it

Use a Punnett square to work out expected ratios. A 3 : 1 ratio comes from Aa × Aa, 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 from AaBb × AaBb. The chi-squared test compares observed and expected numbers; if χ² is less than the critical value, the difference is due to chance.

Hardy–Weinberg: the recessive phenotype frequency is q²; take the square root for q, then p = 1 − q and carriers = 2pq. Mark–release–recapture estimates population size: N = n₁n₂/m.

Example

4% show a recessive trait. Carriers?

q² = 0.04, q = 0.2, p = 0.8

2pq = 0.32

Answer: 32%

Example

50 marked, 40 caught later with 5 marked. N?

50 × 40 ÷ 5

Answer: 400

Common mistakes

  • Using q² as the allele frequency.
  • Using the number of categories as the degrees of freedom.
  • Dividing by O instead of E in χ².

faq.q: When is a chi-squared result significant?
faq.a: When χ² is greater than the critical value at p = 0.05 for the right degrees of freedom: the difference is not due to chance.

faq.q: What does the Hardy–Weinberg principle assume?
faq.a: A large population with random mating and no mutation, migration or selection, so allele frequencies stay the same.
